posts.body:
Hey Folks! Been lurkin' around and wanted to kind of do a thread of games that I've reviewed so far. For those who don't know, I'm a small-potatoes streamer who streams on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays at 8pm EST doing RPG Maker content. Mostly, I do playthroughs of games while commenting on the game, and when I finish I write a review for the game. Whenever someone suggests a new game, I normally put it in a review section where I kind of do a cursory look through the game to make sure it is stream appropriate first.
Below is general information that I will try to keep up to date, but I will be posting here the written reviews I do at the end of each game.

Spoiler:
bio-Synthetica Review
Game Review:
bio-Synthetica (Demo)
Score:
5/5
While it is still in demo stages at this time, there is so much that I can say about this game. The graphics, the sound, the events and combat system. Almost every part of this game was obviously crafted with love to the point that you would be forgiven for thinking it wasn’t made in RPG Maker MV. Honestly, the only thing that gave it away to me as an RPG Maker game was the movement of the character you control.
The story in this game is good and combined with the use of atmosphere and audio, it gives a great oppressive dystopian feel in the sense that things are at their worst and it’s up to you to try and get out to save the world. And I do not mean “dystopian” in the sense of evil corporate overlords, but more in the sense that paranormal  has hit the fan and humanity is either wiped out or on the break of extinction and your little robot was made to help save them, or maybe avenge them.
Oh and that audio was very well used in a scene where you can hear faint whispers from some unseen observers watching you. The sound of movement, the music that plays all adds to the ambiance. There is variety too with the arcade machine that you use to upgrade your skills having a great chip-tune theme.
The radial menu has a nice feel use wise, but at the same time feels very on-brand for the world like it really is part of the HUD that your little robot can see. Speaking of the hud, upgrades you unlock help change the hud in ways that make sense and do not feel intrusive or out of place.
Combat wise it is turned based, meaning not fast paced but certainly requiring planning and a bit of strategy. Some enemies like to stay up and close to punch you in the face, while others prefer ranged attacks that fill up your corrosion meter. That meter by the way does DoT to you when it gets filled one time and can be filled more than once. So keeping in mind your repair items and your status removal items is key in this game. However, that is not the only resource to watch in combat. You have to also balance two other resources. The first being your energy cells that are used for certain abilities and do not recharge during combat but do after. The second one being FDM or Force Drive Module that you build up by attacking in melee and then allows you to use other abilities such as a combo attack or one with fire or lightning infused into it.
Spoiler:
The Seventh Warrior Review
Game Review:
The Seventh Warrior (Demo)
Score:
5/5
Firstly, hot damn this game is long at 6 to 8 hours depending. Amazing graphics and audio, with many of the pieces fitting together so very well. They have a lot of custom work done for not only character designs, but also combat animations and so on with how smooth everything is.
The music is also on point, but the graphics and the sound are only one portion of a game. The UI/Interface that is often used is also very good. There is a bit of a problem with there being no native controller support, but they provide a program that easily integrates in to offset that while they try and find a more permanent solution. This is a bit of a limitation due to using VX Ace as the program they've made this in.
The only major cons tend to be localization issues that they are actively working on as the game is primarily made in German and translated to English. The creator has been super-nice and open to assistance in getting these corrected. The only other thing is if you use the limit breaks too many times in a single battle, then you can cause a memory leak/overload and the game will crash. Thankfully, there is an autosave feature.
I for one am extremely excited to see where this game goes.
Spoiler:
Moonfell: Tides of Aether Review
Game Review:
Moonfell: Tides of Aether (Demo)
Score:
5/5
A love letter if I've ever seen one. Similar to Sword of Saints in a lot of stylizations, but this game is fully reminiscent of the NES days.
The graphics and music are on point and again harkens back to those old days of sitting in front of a CRT TV and playing Final Fantasy or Dragon Warrior. However, this definitely goes above and beyond that old style of gaming with some definite quality of life updates.
Firstly, in combat you do not have to memorize a creature's weakness. When you hit them with it, a small orb under their HP bar will update to show that you had hit them with their weakness and that will stay there for any future encounters with that creature. In example, if a zombie is weak to fire and radiant, then they will have two orbs under their HP bar and when you hit them with fire, one will change to a flame and show for all future encounters.
Additionally in combat there is a feature called Synergy where you can do combo attacks with another character for extra damage or even an added effect. There is also flanking where you guarantee your ability to go first by striking an enemy with an out-of-combat ability and running up to them.
There is a lot of good environmental story telling in this game, and it has a lot of potential considering the demo has a respectable 2 or so hours of gameplay. It is not overly complex from the get-go with how it presents information and provides just enough to get you interested and excited for the full release.
Spoiler:
Scarlet Record Review
Game Review:
Scarlet Record (Demo)
Score:
4.5/5
The game demo alone is a wonderful 6 or so hours long. In the time of playing the demo, I've gotten to see just how much work went into this. The Pros definitely outweight the Cons even though the two Cons are a bit heavy in my opinion.
To start with, the UI throughout the game is wonderful. From the pause menu to the combat wheel, it is smooth easy on the eyes, and easy to understand without needing guesswork.
The music sounds great and is good enough on it's own to just kind of vibe to in the background while doing other things. At no point did it feel like it did not match the tone of the scene.
The combat alone could sell this game. It is obviously the most polished part of it with how the animations, sounds, management of resources and the overall feel of it. Each character has their own unique styles of attacks and strategies that work well with each other to where you don't just rely fully on one character.
This is where the Cons come in though. While not having a "Take All" button for chests is minorly annoying and not worth that much of a mention, the two biggest things are the Maps and the Tutorials.
As of writing this, I have spoken with one of the creators about this, but at the moment the main issues are this. The maps could use more work. The filter and look given to the tiles helps a lot, but it is still the basic RTP that you get straight out of the box. This hurts the game some due to the normal stigma against the basic RTP, but it is combined with the fact that they are using the basic RPG Maker layout system. Tiles or objects feel improperly sized or not properly flushed against others, leading to strange gaps or feeling like the object is too far forward.
The other major issue is the Tutorials. There are so many tutorials early on in the game. The first combat encounter you face has 4 tutorials right off the bat and it brings the game's flow to a screeching hault because it's not an overly interactive tutorial but much more heavy on the reading portion. The next combat has another tutorial and when you get the 3rd member of your team, you get another tutorial or two. These feel like they drag down the flow of the game and cause unnecessary delay/padding.
Aside from this, my final verdict is still a good one. The Pros definitely outweigh the Cons on this as I set this as a 4.5/5 must play.
Spoiler:
Dungeon Rummage - Survival Review
Game Review:
Dungeon Rummage - Survival
Score:
4/5
The game is a cozy play kind of game. Something you get to kill an hour or two. There's no major story, other than you are just trying to gather supplies and build up your little base for better stats.
Secret areas that pop up from time to time for extra materials. Special enemies you can catch and slay for bonus goods.  Combat itself is very simplistic and easy to understand.
In fact, the whole game is simplistic. I do not see this as a bad thing though, as it does have it's finer points. For the cost of the game, and how it is designed purely for you to jump in and kind of turn your brain off to just fight-gather-die-gather more.
Falling in combat is not a game over either. It simply sends you back to your base with a small penalty to all the materials you gathered. The penalty isn't so huge to discourage you either.
For $5 to kill some time, this game only has one major thing that stands out. It needs more music. One track will haunt your dreams with how much it replays.
Score: 4 out of 5 (Add More Music)
Spoiler:
Star Shift Origins Review
Game Review:
Star Shift Origins
Score:
4/5
A nice six and a half-ish hour play. While streaming this we did encounter a couple of bugs that happened after using abilities too much in one combat and another when trying to delete old saves. However, those are minor in the long run as the developer is actively working on fixing these.
The first thing anyone is going to notice and speak out about is the use of AI in this game. Yes, it uses AI primarily for art when it comes to a number of characters and with making some of the javascript plugins. And while I will continue to not like the use of AI, I separated my dislike from this review and playthrough.
The art style for a lot of the character portraits is inconsistent. While it is understandable that the developer was aiming to have them look different in the sense that they are aliens and of different species, the stylization of the art is the issue. Where two people of the same race look different as one has more of an anime/hand drawn look while the other is obviously AI with it's strange shiny layer. Aside from this, there is a small complaint about the lack of tutorials when it comes to skills and getting setup at first.
With the developer constantly going back to fix bugs or to expand on different portions while also working on future titles, it is nice to see that they do take feedback well.
Beyond this the music is good and is nice to listen to, even to just kind of vibe to with it in the background. It is definitely fitting with the more rave/sci-fi sounds for the most part, while some sections have more somber music to fit the scene. Do note, the developer loves the Nova Lighting Plugin considering how much it is used.
Combat is heavily inspired by Suikoden with you having a maximum of 7 party members to work with. Each with their own specialties and some racial abilities that define them from the others. Combat itself is not overly difficult and with some careful planning on your attacks/abilities and learning the proper skills, you can get through most combats easily.
It is nice to see aliens that are humanoid in some sense, but are still very far from human being primary characters. That being said, I do consider them primary characters and not main characters. Character development obviously took a back seat and is secondary to the main story. The game is short at about 6 to 6.5 hours long, developing each character in a meaningful way is not possible. However, developing at least one or two would have certainly been possible. Perhaps more backstory or defining scenes for Carol or Magnus as they appear to be main focuses.
It is obvious that this is a prelude or prologue game to the next ones in the series and is more about setting up the universe that those play in.
Gameplay wise it does alternate between being a traditional RPG  with an ATB and your party versus the enemy party, and a tactics style game depending on what the story requires. This is an interesting twist, and does help as it flows well with what the story needs.
Overall, this game gets a 4 out of 5 and a request to hire a character artist.
Spoiler:
Star Shift Rebellion Review
Game Review:
Star Shift Rebellion
Score:
4/5
Much about what made Star Shift Origins is present here in Star Shift Rebellion. Same systems, same graphics, same mechanics. While a sequel, it is not one that switches things up like many others out there that add in a new mechanic or throws in a different leveling or skill system.
The first thing anyone is going to notice and speak out about is the use of AI in this game, just like in the previous game. Yes, it uses AI primarily for art when it comes to a number of characters and with making some of the javascript plugins. And while I will continue to not like the use of AI, I separated my dislike from this review and playthrough.
There is still a small complaint about the lack of tutorials when it comes to skills and getting setup at first, and with the game being longer that the previous one, it can sometimes become a little tedious dealing with the skill tree for 7 party members. Having to go through and check each one's skills and abilities to see if you have enough points for something or if you missed a critical skill.
Combat has not changed from the previous title of Star Shift Origins and there is an interesting bug where your counter ability may go off on an ally. However, the developer is working to fix that.
At least the developer is constantly going back to fix bugs or to expand on different portions while also working on future titles, it is nice to see that they do take feedback well.
Beyond this the music is good and is nice to listen to, even to just kind of vibe to with it in the background. It is definitely fitting with the more rave/sci-fi sounds for the most part, even in some battles or the casino lounge that makes me still question if androids dream of electric sheep.
This game is definitely packed with much more lore and information. You get a nice look into how a number of the different alien species came about, where it turns out that some are not really aliens, but animals that were elevated to sentience.
Gameplay wise it does alternate between being a traditional RPG  with an ATB and your party versus the enemy party, and a tactics style game depending on what the story requires. This is an interesting twist, and does help as it flows well with what the story needs.
Overall, this game gets a 4 out of 5 and a request to hire an artist.
Spoiler:
Relics of Aurelia Review
Game Review:
Relics of Aurelia
Score:
4/5
A giant puzzle of a game that is an interesting take on how progression is done. It also must be stated that the RTP being used is the basic barebone, the rest of the game makes up for this with the quality of the content.
A year later from when I first played it, it was definitely a fresh breath of air of a game! Instead of focusing on grinding up levels, you are trying to find the right equipment or "Relic" that holds the power you need.
This doesn't mean that fighting the weaker random battles is not rewarding though. They do tend to drop crafting materials that can be used to improve your equipment if you get enough of them with the right recipe.
The titular Relics are unique in their own, as they provide both buffs and debuffs. A risk vs reward customization is a novel concept, but is combined with the fact that you may have no idea what a Relic does unless you find the corresponding tablet that tells you. There are also tablets that let you know about a particular monster that you must defeat in order to progress. All this to say that exploration is rewarded and is critical to the game.
With small amounts of lore given to you upfront, the real meat of the story is also rewarded with exploration. Going into towns and speaking with NPCs or interacting with bookshelves to read about an event from ages pass or even to gather recipes to improve gear.
As for negatives, the game needs more in the ways of maps to make the world feel bigger and more fleshed out with more side quests. There's also the issue with grinding for materials, as the drop rate is too low to feel like it is worth going after so you can craft improved versions of the Relics.
There is also much needed in polish when it comes to the menu and the key items, to where when you get a relic's recipe it is more easily accessible to see what the recipe requires and what benefit there is from completing it. As the current setup does not flow as well as it could possibly flow.
Final score is a 4 out of 5, make some more content!
Spoiler:
Shadow Seeker Review
Game Review:
Shadow Seeker
Score:
4/5
The game nails the atmosphere of a noir story with the sound design alone. Always bordering on creepy or unsettling as you can hear monsters faintly in the backgrounds or something that sounds like it's following close behind.
Do you like Resident Evil? I mean the OLD Resident Evil games, because this is definitely paying homage to that. Mysterious happenings and the dead rising to tear at your flesh. You are on the case for a missing persons and possible homicide when you are thrusted into this situation.
The controls could use some work as it does not have full controller support so keyboard is the way to go. This is honestly the only glaring issue with the game, as a controller has functions for aiming, moving shooting and accessing the menu. But running and using the knife are right out. This makes things very difficult as there are even advanced movements such as running and dodging that can only be done with the keyboard, but the button placements are honestly not great.
Ignoring this issue with controls, this game does a lot of things right. As mentioned before the atmosphere is on point. Map layouts and mapping is great! The mansion feels like a mansion that's been built by a paranoid madman, which fits with the story. The constant sound of rain feels as if the world feels like it's trying to drown out the horrors you unfold.
With the controls issue being the only thing wrong from what I have been able to play, this game is a solid 4 out of 5. If they are able to get full controller support up, this has the potential to be a 5 out of 5 for me.
Spoiler:
Chronicles of Veldoria Review
Game Review:
Chronicles of Veldoria
Score:
1/5
The only game I've revisited for a second time around and gave an updated review. The Dev had reached out to me in regards to this, stating they did a lot of overhauling to the game since the last time I reviewed it.
That being said, I still do not feel like the $3.99 price tag is justifiable for something that is in their own words "early access". Primarily because I do not feel like what is available to play at the moment is of quality to justify the price. Please do note, I have no issue with you charging for your work or for your game, but at the same time remember that the moment you put a price tag on something, you open your product up to a higher level of scrutiny and critique.
The game itself the first time and the second time has a "death by a thousand cuts" kind of feeling. It feels like a conglomeration of ideas without any satisfying substance. Much of this game feels stilted and unnatural.
Tiling/Mapping is still broken in several spots. Ranging from not being able to pass through something you should be able to, to passing through things you shouldn't be able to. Spacing between where the character can move and where it appears they should be able to move as well.
You can now scan enemies, but now if you use the item on certain enemies it doesn't work. If you use it as the last thing of your turns, it breaks the game.
Some events trigger without telling you who/what/when/where. You can still get the "HELP ME!!" event but no direction as to which way to go to resolve it. The scene were you find Sara, the attacks are going so fast and so much, it's annoying to listen to, but you because you didn't know which direction to run, it may take you a few minutes to finally find and save her. Thankfully she appears indestructible until you go to save her.
While it is nice that there is some kind of "interaction" between the characters when they are just wandering around, it doesn't feel natural or even organic. More of "Oh, you've walked around with me for 300 steps, time to ask me some questions!" The writing needs a lot of work, but also how it's presented stops you and you can't proceed until you make a selection.
Well, at least the awful AI voices got removed.
Spoiler:
Nightmarena Review
Game Review:
Nightmarena
Score:
5/5
An interesting game that no does not allow you to take passive strategies.
It's turn based but also timing base with it's combat. Your fights are based upon if you can duck, jump or backstep away from an incoming attack by reading the attack right. There is some that even have faint little details between the two that let you know, like a sound clue or a certain item turned upwards or downwards. However, when it's your own turn you must act quickly or you'll do nothing more than a simple punch!
The combat in this feels smooth, very good and balanced, with it increasingly getting difficult as the game progresses. Some enemies may prove more difficult than others for you depending on not only how well you can read their attacks, but how well you can react in time! With enough victories you get the currency Energi to trade for upgrades to your stats or even buffs, and those first few battles will be easy peasy.
Combat alone is not the only thing though. There's plenty of lore and story sprinkled about and given to you in short bursts of dialogue versus long winded exposition. Each NPC that speaks with you having their own personalities and it shows through their dialogue. The knights speaking with a ye old English with "Thous" and "Doths" while the Nagas speak with the typical (but still comical) overpronounced S. Even the fairy that ends up helping you has their own uniqueness in how they address the player with their own unique butchering of their last name.
With everything, I give this game a solid 5 out of 5 with the note of get me a full game.
Spoiler:
Thrall Review
Game Review:
Thrall
Score:
4/5
The game has an interesting story without question. You and your team of Vampire Hunters are trying to reclaim your lost ally by gathering a greater force to hunt down not just any blood suckers, but rather THE Blood Suckers.
Combat has a weird mix between an ATB and turn based, to where it is not fully clear which one actually takes priority. Skill cooldowns are also rather unforgiving and can make it feel like a punishment for using them. The item loss and gold loss you experience when defeated is rather soul crushing. That being said, I've not encountered any other negatives in this game.
Equipment stats and types are randomized enough to where you can get lots of good weapons and armor, some that add permanent (and sometimes vital) buffs! This can also mean you may not get the equipment type you want for a bit. Such as with Lionel's skills being best suited to use swords, having him equip spears is not that great of build for him.
Speaking of skills, each party member has their own unique skill tree that dictates how they are played. Though be careful when using said skills, many of them have a long cool down at first until you get the right skill or the right equipment to help cut this down. Unfortunately, this can lead many to hoard their skills and make combats take much longer or lead them to take more damage. Some skills can easily deal with one foe, but if you use it then you do not have it again for many turns. These skills also do not reset when combat ends, and will continue to be on cooldown into the next combat.
Loss of items when you perish, is a big progression hit as you now how to grind up money or supplies in order to try and fight against what killed you again. However, at the time of writing this the Dev has spoke about how they can see about adjusting these main negatives to not impact the game as much.
Until these adjustments take place, this game is a solid 4 out of 5 with a lot of great potential!
Spoiler:
Meta Revelations - Armour of the Abyss Review
Game Review:
Meta Revelations - Armour of the Abyss
Score:
5/5
Meta Revelations - Armour of the Abyss, definitely worth a cheese toasty. The game is wonderfully made in visual aesthetics alone. There's always a love for art made by the one who is also developing the game, as well as when it still has the hand drawn look.
The art style and visuals stay nice and consistent throughout while combining a mixture of fantasy and a touch of sci-fi-modernism. Many showing a creepy, otherworldly look to monsters while the humans look a little worn down by the lives they lead.
Adena's past isn't forced to you but is rather given through bites as she pieces it together, and they use the visuals well as they combine them with the adage of showing and not telling. They show that Adena struggles with a sense of identity, a hidden past, and something that dwells within her. They show that Fenrir is remorseful for not being able to keep their promise.
The music is also wonderful in the opening menu alone, but as you play it adds to the atmosphere where the presentation of music, visuals, and environmental storytelling blend very well together.
The game does have a minor fault in that sometimes it is not consistent in whether or not character art is supposed to be showing or not in one or two instances. However, this is a very minor thing and the text boxes do sometimes change and needs to be a bit clearer as to why also in one or two instances. Neither are to the point it is distracting or rampant throughout the whole demo.
Still, this game is great and can still be considered good running for a 5 out of 5, finish the damn game and fix inconsistencies.
Spoiler:
Soul Survivor: Trials of the Goddess Review
Game Review:
Soul Survivor: Trials of the Goddess
Score:
5/5
Keeping with the themes of the early NES days of JRPGs, the 8-bit retro look and sprite work on the overworld, with the attention to detail of someone who is passionate about the genre works so well with this treat of a game. Twice I played this game on stream and went over my usual 2hr limit because I was just enjoying it that much.
Some may look at it and think, "Oh, it's not that long." and they would be roughly correct. Though the length of the game is not what truly defines how you should measure this game. No, it is the high amounts of replayability. You can go through the game multiple times, trying different combinations of classes, skills, items, equipment and have unique playthroughs each time. Plus, with the difficulty you will find times that your build might not work and you have to start again.
While it doesn't have a true-save deleting mechanic like other rogue-likes, instead opting for an honor-system where you can delete your save and start over or continue from your save and keep going with your build to focus on seeing the rest of the story. I feel like this makes it appeal for both those who do and those who do not like that hardcore aspect of starting over every game over.
Without giving spoilers of the story, lore is given in bite sizes and sprinkled about in interactive ruins. Slowly revealing the truth of the island and the curse you are there to destroy.
With all of this combined, I score this game a perfect 5 out of 5. Damn it Runelight Owl, you sonuva, you did it again.
Spoiler:
Dungeon Rummage - Tiqee's Escape Review
Game Review:
Dungeon Rummage - Tiqee's Escape
Score:
4.5/5
Another Dungeon Rummage game! This means lots of crafting and gathering what is needed in order to get by.
Combat is rather straight forward with a decent strategy of building your bots to do a lot of the work for you. Meaning as you progress through, you start taking on more of a support role to the real damage dealers. You spend your resources to refill or repair the bots while they take the damage for you.
Exploration is definitely rewarded in this game as you will find many hidden rooms where you can gather extra supplies and maybe even an item that permanently increases your skills. The hidden rooms themselves don't stick out like sore thumbs, but at the same time don't blend in so well that you can't tell where they are.
Sadly, much like the other Dungeon Rummage game that I've played and is available at this time, it's too damn short! Sure, it's a $3 game and I shouldn't be demanding more than what I got, the fact remains that because it feels like nothing more than a taste of what is to come in another game, the ending feels unresolved.
The art styles have a little bit of a concern as the art for Tiqee and the bots do not match the art styles of well.. all of the others. Both the monsters you fight and the twins Gabbo and Gobbo are different.
Well, at least the music isn't hauntingly repetitive.
Score: 4.5 out of 5. Give me more.
Spoiler:
Silver Daze (Demo) Review
Game Review:
Silver Daze (Demo)
Score:
5/5
Silver Daze is an apt name for this game.
The retro feel of not only the pixel graphics but also the themes and stylizations of the world. It perfectly conveys a time of life where things were not so technologically advanced but also was not so simple.
The music is good to vibe to and helps with keeping up-beat, or just being there to vibe to as you sit in the dark with the CRT TV being your night light.
What stands out the most though is the story. While the demo only gives you about a 2hr taste, it is more than enough to get you ready for more. A story of being trapped in those adolescent years of being just about to leave high school but not feeling quite ready for adulthood. With three characters perfectly representing different views.
Pinn, paralyzed by the fear of the uncertain future and multitude of choices. He clings to what he has in hopes it will last just a little bit longer, not wanting to lose any of it to the endless march of time.
Geo, a vibe of a character who has accepted how his life is and is fine with drifting and floating along with it. He is loyal and wise, but certainly carries a bit of reluctance to charge forward while being dismissive of the idea of being stuck.
Kani, driven to push forward to a future she believes she deserves as she has worked so hard for it. A bit scared of her past, but is not afraid of pushing forward or of forging her own path forward.
The three work well together with their dynamic of personalities, and this works into the combat as well. Each represented by a different color they use cards matching their color to deal damage or use special abilities. The combat itself is a little simplistic but in a very good way. It adds a layer of strategy not seen in many other turn based RPGs in the sense that you get to see who is most likely going to get hit first by their Aggro rating. All the while the color of the card you use is like a form of rock-paper-scissors.
My score is a strong 5 out of 5 with a simple demand. Finish the damn game so I can play more!
Spoiler:
Leyline Chronicles Review
Game Review:
Leyline Chronicles
Score:
4/5
Leyline Chronicles, a good RPG at a decent price.
This game had its ups and downs as you play through it, and while I played through it, the dev made several changes and updates behind me. So while I was able to give my honest feelings and views, things have improved since playing.
The first thing to note is that the combat of this game is solid. The chain system where you can link together multiple attacks to get a special move or just build up points needed for a later combo, it's great. There is some visual noise some may feel is a bit too much, but overall the strategy that goes into making sure you have the right party members and leveling up their skills and gear is more than worth it.
The music is a vibe when it comes to some scenes and the intro menu, but also it kicks up into a higher gear with battles and even more so with boss battles. You can go from something relatively chill into something energizing and ready to throw down with some horrid abomination from beyond the void.
However, there are some weak points we have to address with this game. The first being story beats and plot points that are often feeling a little underused. The dev has talked about refining this much more and better in the sequel and has gone into this game to help restore content that was cut that helps better flesh out these scenes. So while this is good, it doesn't fix the issue there are times where the side quests do not feel like full/real quests but more of "Go talk to this guy." and there are still some underused plot points that could help more with defining the characters and developing them.
The other weak point is that the world does not feel as lived in or ready to be explored. There's a fair amount to do, but at the same time many NPCs just have a single line above their head or there's environmental story telling spots on the overworld map that you cannot interact with but feel like you should be able to. There's also spots that look like locations, but you don't really get to go in them.
Overall though, the game is still good and worth a play through. For me, it gets a solid 4 out of 5.

Azarine Heart Review
Game Review:
Azarine Heart
Score:
2/5
Disclaimer: I really enjoyed the world building and story potential of Azarine Heart, but this review focuses on the problems of the game.
Azarine Heart has an interesting basis for a plotline and lots of potential, but that is also what kills it for me.
My first gripe is no real controller support. You can do conversations and dashing with the controller, but no combat or abilities. So you might as well use the awkward keyboard controls that don't really work well for an Action RPG. Plus, dashing is not the most effective way of travelling, because that's the dodge key that's not on the controller.
My second gripe is a two-parter about combat, as it is a major thing in the game. No matter the difficulty, you can skip random encounters in the overworld by simply mashing the dodge key and backstepping. Meaning you can travel from one side of the map to the other by mashing dodge and only stopping to change directions and not once encounter a single random encounter. The second part of this gripe is that while I love Action RPGs, the RPG Maker system is not a good system for Action RPGs.
While I hear there is a new plugin out that is much smoother and better for Action RPGs in RPG Maker, this game came out before then. Where you have an issue where certain animations take priority over others and there is no animation cancelling. Attacking and Moving for instance. Attack animations take priority over Moving animations, to where if you do the inputs for both either on top of or too closely together, your character will only attack. This includes when you are just wanting to change directions to swing at a new enemy. This means that you will need to heavily slow down your reactions and inputs in order to properly play, which is an antithesis of what an Action RPG is about. The best strategy appears to be to just dump stat points into health and attack and face tank while standing in a spot where enemies need to come to you and hope you hit them more than they hit you.
My third gripe is about the main story. While I did try some of the side quests, that were a little lackluster early on, the main story feels underwhelming not in what it is about but rather how you are a part of it. It tells you to ask the locals, and through a few dialogue options with the right NPC it will eventually tell you to go to one of three different cities of Eastwatch, Oakcross or Blackmark. I ended up going to Oakcross as it was much closer, where I talked to more NPCs before one told me to speak to a particular NPC, where I was then told to leave and go to Eastwatch to talk to a different NPC, halfway across the map. Once I got there, they gave me a book to deliver back to Oakcross to the person who told me to go to Eastwatch, who then tells me to go to take a nap and then to go back to Eastwatch to try and find a scholar in the Mage's Guild.
Who in the Mage's Guild you ask?  if I know, you aren't given a name, just that they are in the Mage's Guild. So I go to the Mage's Guild and talk to every NPC available and not a single one says, "Oh, you need a scholar? Second floor, their name is <insert name>." Like you work and live with these people, and you can't be bothered to roughly know who does what or who might know? I understand wanting your players to explore your open world, but having this as the first leg of your main story is just down right disrespectful of your player's time. I would akin it to Morrowind, but Morrowind had the decency to give you clear "Go here and find/talk to <NPC>." and when you get to that city you can ask almost every NPC about what or who you are looking for and they will give some kind of information.
Potential means nothing if not properly acted upon. A rock has potential to be thrown, broken, smoothed, polished and/or refined into a statuette or some other object. To say it has potential is nice, but it ignores the rough parts that must be fixed. With these three main gripes hitting so early on, I am not willing to play the game to completion. With combat and controls being so unfun, I would not be able to give it a proper review.

Tower Song
Game Review:
Tower Song
Score:
3.8/5
Tower Song is an interesting game. The story and the world building was enjoyable from start to finish. The ability to move about the map and between areas felt rather rewarding and it was interesting that certain items or paths were blocked out completely as the hero that you chose to play as determined what was available.
This adds to a large level of re-playability, but can also make it feel like the player is missing out on things because they are not able to explore as much without going back through with a different hero each time. The use of Milestone levels versus grinding/exp levels is certainly an interesting touch not really seen in video games these days, and it is rather refreshing.
Crafting doesn't feel like it is too much, and while it is the best way to progress equipment wise, it also doesn't feel like it is reaching its full potential.
The maps are well done and fun to navigate through, and the world at times does feel lived in with either NPCs or just how things are laid out. However, it does have a glaring flaw in it.
Tower Song is far from a bad game, but it does have some pain points that hammer at the score the most. Ignoring the few moments where you clip through or bypass a spot entirely due to a mapping error, the main issue with it tends to be the combat.
Combat does have some nice, flaring animations on the screen for spells, abilities, etc. However, the image of the enemies you are fighting do not react to the damage or change after their health gets below a certain point. Instead they remain rather static throughout and while this is often seen in 8bit, 16bit, and 32bit retro games, it does not work as much here. With the higher definition of graphics, a part of you expects the image to change, but it never does. Additionally, while the battlebacks look nice, they don't always sit well as sometimes it feels like enemies are just floating there.
Combat also has an issue where there is an issue with scaling/balancing. Sometimes you go into combat and wipe the enemy team out in 1 to 2 actions, but then the fight shortly after is very difficult. This makes the combat feel skewed one way or the other, which can be dangerous of either making your players bored or frustrated depending.
The times it is skewed against you it is increasingly frustrating. One combat I spent the first few rounds doing nothing and just watching my party being wiped out because almost every enemy had stun locked each member two times in a row. Other times the enemies just had a very annoying AoE that they spammed almost every round, combined with some enemies that get 2 to 3 actions per round. Some of which are just automatic heals/shields/AoE damage.
In short, the game has a good story and for the most part is nice to play through. However, the combat needs some heavy rebalancing.

Scarmonde Review
Game Review:
Scarmonde
Score:
5/5
To say Scarmonde is a good game is an understatement. I feel like this game is a great game, with it's aesthetics calling back to the old days of NES/SNES JRPGs.
I don't mean that just visually though. This game has a lot of great pixel art from the tiling to the monsters. Reminding you of the old days playing the first Final Fantasy and Dragon Warrior. The music combines with this where it's got a retro feel to it and at some parts goes harder than expected with the chiptune sound. I'm still rocking out to some of the later dungeons' music where you can just stand there and listen.
Though keep in mind this game does have some quality of life bonuses over those old retro games while it pays homage to them. The skill system is rather straight forward and rewards customization and building up how you want, but at the same time is not so complex that you feel a sense of choice paralysis that you can in games that go too hard into the skill system. Combining with the right equipment, you can have a character that is not like any other or even an entirely different playthrough each go around.
The story is also good in the sense that you get bits and pieces of lore through interacting with the NPCs you come across, but nothing is fully forcing you to slog through long exposition or dialogue. You get a sense of the story, and the slow realization of the truth of Scarmonde.
High amounts of re-playability aside, the game will challenge you and even punish you for not accounting for building up your resistances. I still shake my fist angrily at the monsters that spammed debuffs and curses, making a straightforward fight into a challenge. However, that is not a negative in my opinion. Having a game that can challenge you is always great, and the fact that it does this as well as having a great amount of exploration that is rewarded, this game hits all the marks perfectly.
To me, this game was worth every penny I paid for it.

Yggdrasil Chronicles - A Record of Valkadia (Early Access) Review
Game Review:
Yggdrasil Chronicles - A Record of Valkadia (Early Access)
Score:
2.5/5
Yggdrasil Chronicles - A Record of Valkadia, I think this game wins the competition for the longest name of a game I've reviewed so far.
There is a lot going on with this game that unfortunately makes me think it is just rather average. It's not terrible, but it's not standing out and making itself great either. There are times where it gets in its own way.
Mechanics wise, it is a rather straight forward JRPG game even with the combat. However, it does have interesting mechanics where a spell or two has a dual purpose. Such as healing allies or damaging enemies depending on who you cast it on. Though the one in particular I am speaking of is almost never good offensively. Here is the exact text of this is the spell you start with called Voodoo Cure. Setting aside my dislike of the name for obvious reasons, the spell literally states:
"Restores HP to one ally by an amount of 50 + 2x MAT (x). If target's HP is lower than 50%, it will get extra HP recovery equal to 10% of its MHP, but consumes extra MP equal to 10% of the target's missing HP. If the user's MP is lower than the target's mentioned missing HP, the effectiveness of extra HP recovery is lowered respectively. If target is an Undead or an enemy, deals 100% of your MAT as Darkness damage to it. Can be cast on either ally or enemy."
In short, it heals better when the target is at lower health, but it costs more to heal them. So don't heal them if they are lower health. If you use it on an enemy, then it's not going to do much damage comparatively. So don't use it on an enemy, especially if they resist Darkness.
This is just one example of the mechanics going to a needlessly complex level. The character Lucia is much worse in my opinion.
The other two major pain points for the game is its tutorials and pacing. The tutorials often are many and needless. Thankfully the dev has made it to where you can skip them now, but they mostly can be summed up into 2 to 3 lines from an NPC without having to go through a whole tutorial showing you how to do something.
In regards to pacing, the story "jumps" or "sprints" through sections of development character wise or narratively. Where it can honestly be hard to keep up for what is being spoken about, and there are times where it also feels like the main character Morrigan is a little bit of a Mary Sue with worrying levels of blind trust or blind mistrust with no real reason given. There is also an issue in pacing between map scenes, where it's told but not really shown how far you've been travelling. Or worse, where you are told to go in a direction to get to a city and it's one transition screen away through a short walk from gate to gate.
As mentioned it's just average at a 2.5/5 but it can still be redeemed and worked on to improve. So I'm hopeful, at least.

Noblesse Oblige: Legacy of the Sorcerer Kings
Game Review:
Noblesse Oblige: Legacy of the Sorcerer Kings
Score:
2/5
Noblesse Oblige: Legacy of the Sorcerer Kings is the game that takes the current title for the longest game title that I've reviewed. Seriously, that's a lot to say. I will say that at this time, I'm only 8hrs in and I have no plans of continuing further.
I completed the prologue and where I stopped, I can only assume is the end of Chapter 1 or very near it. However, a certain topic and the romanticization of the certain topic, has completely removed any interest I have in continuing playing. Before I get into that, I did want to be fair and judge it based upon its merits before finishing my scoring.
Firstly, this game would do much better as a Visual Novel or just a book. While there are choices that one can make in the game that vary the story, the story itself is so dense with dialogue and scenes that legitimately are written like pages of a book, an RPG game like this does not fit.
The pacing is also awful in my honest opinion. By pacing I mean the long stretches of dialogue, in some cases where some a conversation kind of repeats itself, or even could have been summed up with way less words. With sometimes a simple, small break for one to two combat followed by 30 to 40 minutes more of, you guessed it, dialogue. But worry not, because it is then followed by more combat that will just drag on. And I do mean, drag on. The combat itself is rather quick thankfully, and strategy for them for the most part is well balanced in difficulty. It is purely the sheer amount of combat. Because it is not 3 to 4 battles, it is more like 10 to 15. I did not know it was possible for something to make my Adderall to wear off faster.
And in honesty, there is no reason for combat at all. Because there is only a limited number of combats available. Meaning there is a cap on the rewards and on the experience that you can get. There is no grinding in this game, so why is there even combat that hands out experience? Just take the experience points away and do a milestone leveling system.
Much of this game is well written, it has interesting story beats, and the charm of scenes being replaced by literal pages of a book, marks this as unique. The characters having actual art (but only some characters) and their own special quirks for both in combat and in story is also interesting. This game has a lot going for it, but it is flawed. And there is one flaw I just can't ignore.
The Steam page does reference mature content, stating that it does contain general mature themes, including non-explicit descriptions of violence, political intrigue, realpolitik, implicit sexual intimacy, references to attempted sexual assault and coercion, and the use of fictional addictive drugs. However, they should drop the attempted.
The scene I ended on was where the character Ligaea had been kidnapped and prepared to be used in a demonic ritual. She was drugged with an addictive aphrodisiac and it is laid bear that the bindings to her are linked to her being a virgin. The only way to save her is to have sex with her. The characters Alexander and Ariadne both admit, to each other, that if they were to wake Ligaea and ask for her consent before going through with their plan to free her by having sex with her, that she likely would not be of sound enough mind due to the drug. They also did not have time for the drug to wear off, and the drug could also kill her if she did not have her lust satiated. They also couldn't just take her away, else the bindings would kill her.
In 8 hours of playing, this is the third reference to rape. Because when you first meet Ligaea, you save her from a fellow classmate who is going to rape her. Alexander arriving just in time, it seems. The second time you are in the next chapter, where two guards had kidnapped a young girl and you again arrive just in time. This certainly set up two red flags that show an intentional pattern. Someone is going to be raped, but Alexander will swoop in to save the day. The third time, Alexander is the rapist. There is no sugar coating it, there is no justification. Alexander is willing to "sacrifice" this "purity" to save Ligaea, and while the game does not go into detail (thank the ing Gods), it is still heavily implied that the deed was done.
Not only was this a straight up betrayal of the story thus far, considering the constant teasing will-they-won't-they going on between Alexander and Ligaea, only to have it tossed aside with this. Yes, Ligaea wanted it when she was sober and not drugged up. But they never went beyond a line, and having drugs and a ritual thrown into the mix, betrays that build up with the kind of flair of, "Well it was gonna happen eventually."
And why was this scene needed for the story? Ah, yes. To bring an Incubus into the world to where you then get the choice of making a deal with it or not. The deal? You let it loose into the world and it will hand over the guy who made this whole scene possible for you to kill him. Or, you can fight the Incubus, with no promise that justice will be had.
I like fantasy. I like dark and horror fantasy books. I know that reality is often far harsher than the imagined words put to paper. However, that does not mean I should overlook the romanticization of such a topic.
Score: 2/5 Write a book instead.
Spoiler:
Crimson Snow Deluxe Review
Game Review:
Crimson Snow Deluxe
Score:
3/5
Crimson Snow Deluxe, a game that goes too wordy for words.
There is a lot I can say about this game in both the good and bad categories. The combat is very simplistic for the build that I played, and from my understanding the game is still getting overhauls in regards to a lot of features. Still, it is easy to see how much games like Undertale and Deltarune heavily inspired this game. My experience for writing this review is based upon getting 2 endings for the game.
Unfortunately, it is hard to weigh this due to some parts counting as both a pro and a con for this game. For instance the story itself. It is a pro in the sense that it is unique and that there are multiple paths and endings that you can get for your playthrough, making each playthrough possibly unique. It is a con that it does at times feel like a first or second draft of a story, and your saves get deleted at the end of a playthrough.
There are times where certain paths are not clear, or where it feels like you achieved an ending, but Phantom Scott did not approve of it so he deleted your save and made you start over. Or where player agency was taken away due to Phantom Scott. There are times for the sake of plot that player agency should be or can be taken away, but you have to be careful when it is done and how you frame it is also very important. Otherwise, it can feel like a betrayal to the player or even leave a bad taste in their mouth due to the experience.
Save deletion for a narratively driven game with multiple endings by the way, is rather hardcore, and can turn many players away. Not saying there are not games with similar or the same feature, just simply that if a game is very dialogue and story driven, while not being a roguelike, then it can again make players unhappy. Especially if a particular choice gets them an unexpected ending, and now they have to start over from the beginning. Sometimes, we like going back to a previous save to see if a choice would have made the difference, without going through the whole game again.
The map is a bit of a struggle at times, where this game could definitely use a fresh/new coat of paint versus the RTP being used. As in some parts it clashes with the hand drawn aesthetic of the characters. Lots of small rooms as well, but very few with anything of actual note in them. And due to the sizing of the maps and how easy it is to transition from one kingdom to another, it is hard to believe this is a full world.
There is also the issue where the suspension of disbelief, where you as the player are able to set aside small details to fully enjoy the story, becomes difficult. Purely due to a few narrative choices, and they tend to stack up. One of the big ones that sticks out is Foreline, the kingdom you start in, has all the food. Combined with the low populations of each kingdom, where they barely get over 100 all together, it makes it difficult to believe that there are even kingdoms left. Or why everyone hasn't simply moved to Foreline, as that is where the food is. In fact, it is flatly mentioned by the other kingdoms that they have to trade with Foreline to get food.
The interactions between the player and Phantom Scott, including the "pets" section, does not feel satisfying. Especially since you do not get any kind of notification that his happiness gets too low, and then he will just  with the game. The added thought that he may just straight up disobey in combat because these got too low, is also a drawback. And from my time playing, I did not see a benefit to this entire section.
However, I cannot ignore the elephant in the room. The game is meant to be set in a Medieval-Renaissance like era of the 1530s. As mentioned, the game is dialogue heavy and unfortunately the dialogue is going to turn a lot of players away almost immediately. The reason being that it is a strange form of Shakespearian wording. Not just the use of doths, thous, and such, but even pulling many words that would be archaic even to the time of Shakespeare.
It goes without saying that the use of archaic words in modern times does not work, because not many people would know the exact translation of the word, may struggle with the word entirely, and when you make paragraphs of these words one after another, it can be taxing. No one wants to have to translate the game themselves while trying to play and enjoy the game.
For example, rampant use of the words "what", "wot", "not", and "aught" right next to each other in the same sentence. Where "wot" means "to know", "know", "have knowledge", or "have knowledge of" depending on the usage. The word "aught" meaning "anything or any part of" such as "I do not know aught of this." The word "hie" meaning "to hurry", "to hasten", or "to go quickly" once again based upon context. These among many others are thrown at you often with many other nouns and proper nouns that makes it hard to distinguish at times. I feel I only did as well as I did during my streams of the game due to my background and love for Shakespeare. Even then, as it is mentioned in a very easy to miss book/entry, there are some words that do not mean the same compared to ones that we would know if we are familiar with the language of the time period. However, your average person would likely get lost and possibly uninstall due to not understanding the plot or what was being said.
The biggest point against this game is honestly the language. It would be fine if one or two of the NPCs spoke this way, as they could just be labeled as "weird" or from a culture where that is more normal. However, it is every dialogue in the game. Even the written dialogue has the dropping of letters where it is written like it is being spoken and not like it was properly written. It acts like a gate that keeps out potential players, simply by the fact that it becomes an accessibility issue.
Mixing verbiage, languages, and even using archaic words is fine, when used properly and sparingly. Changing a simple phrase like "Sir, doth thou wot aught at all about Maxwell?" to "Sir, doth thou know aught of Maxwell?" still has a bit of the same old style of speaking but it flows much better when spoken/read, as you are no longer jumping from "wot" to "aught" where (if you are like me) you may end up saying "wahtat".
FFXIV is a good example of using such flowery, poetic language sparingly in the character Urianger. Who speaks in this kind of prose and form, but he is (if memory serves) literally the only person who does this. And it is even pointed out as to being just an odd thing that Urianger does. By using such a character sparingly but also in a manner in which that his phrasing and verbiage doesn't distract or slow down the scenes due to it being simplistic enough to easily understand, Urianger becomes a rather well liked and unique character. I feel that Crimson Snow Deluxe would benefit greatly if it were to take this kind of approach. That way it is more easily understood for a wider range of audience.
All in all, I score this game a 3 out of 5: "Attempt once more, when thou hast honed thy skills with parchment and quill."
Spoiler:
Kingdom of Nyabur Review
Game Review:
Kingdom of Nyabur
Score:
4/5
Kingdom of Nyabur, an adventure through a world on the brink of collapse.
With an intro movie that has the animation style of early 2000s flash and honestly makes me think back to Saturday morning cartoons, this is one of the games that I was looking forward to playing.
There is a lot in this game that shows the love and passion that went into making it. The art style of the characters have a nice, hand drawn look that keeps its unique feeling, and doesn't clash with the rest of the game. The music is good but there are some parts where it does not feel quite right, but there are far more instances where it hits just right, especially for bosses.
However, it is the story and the content that is the most important. I spent roughly 34 hours playing, with a few wanderings here and there, but primarily focusing on the main quest. From what I was able to experience, there was quality time spent, not just time wandering from place to place or doing a lot of needless grinding. At no point did I feel woefully under-leveled for an area but I never really felt over-leveled for them either. There are certainly some spots to clear up in regards to clarifying direction for certain quests, or even some of the puzzles that you will encounter.
Speaking of puzzles, this game has them. What is even better, is that even the later puzzles in the game, will have you using tools that you got early in the game. This is always good, as it makes tools no longer a one-use kind of thing or a one-dungeon kind of thing. Instead, you swap between them for solving a puzzle or progressing through a dungeon, sometimes having to use two at the same time in order to proceed.
But let us talk about the story. You are playing as Prince Arvin, who ed up. In order to avenge those close to you, to right some wrongs, and to save your kingdom of Nyabur, you travel the world and to the other kingdoms seeking aid. Along the way, you pick up party members who are diverse enough in their designs and in their backgrounds to where you don't have just a party of humans. You have the enigmatic Logva, who you learn later on is a cat-folk. The wise Iris, who is from a race of bird-folk and honestly has my favorite limit break. Gaklu, who is actually a cross between a goblin and an orc. I won't go too deep into each of them, to avoid spoilers, but I will say that the diverse cast of 8 members of this main crew is nice to see.
However, having such a large main cast does have its drawbacks. There are times where it feels like more can be done with the characters as they feel underused in some parts. Thankfully, the dev was in the chat during my streams, and is very receptive to feedback. As such, they confirmed on some of the ideas of how to better utilize the characters and get their motivations, origins, and so on a little more into the light. As well as better showing the dynamic between the party members, while also fixing bugs that I encountered during my playthrough.
I was also happy to see that while there were kingdoms that were specifically for certain races, such as a dwarven kingdom, a mermaid kingdom, an elven kingdom, etc. Not all of the kingdoms had specifically just one race. Some had a mixing of two to three in them, and it helped show that this wasn't the overly stereotypical fantasy setup.
With solid (but not complex or super innovative) combat thrown on top where you can swap out characters mid combat, some who have abilities that stack extremely well with each other, and each perfectly filling a role, you are able to get a solid game plan down for taking on any encounter you come across. Some fights will require a bit more magic than blade, while others will require you to make sure you are prepared to power through.
It still has some spots to grow at and I am excited to see what the final version looks like and the following it develops. In all, I believe that the current build of Kingdom of Nyabur gets a solid 4 out of 5: "I still can't understand French."

Edit: Moved to original post.
Game Review:
Chronicles of Veldoria
Score:
1/5
Spoiler:
Chronicles of Veldoria Review
The only game I've revisited for a second time around and gave an updated review. The Dev had reached out to me in regards to this, stating they did a lot of overhauling to the game since the last time I reviewed it.
That being said, I still do not feel like the $3.99 price tag is justifiable for something that is in their own words "early access". Primarily because I do not feel like what is available to play at the moment is of quality to justify the price. Please do note, I have no issue with you charging for your work or for your game, but at the same time remember that the moment you put a price tag on something, you open your product up to a higher level of scrutiny and critique.
The game itself the first time and the second time has a "death by a thousand cuts" kind of feeling. It feels like a conglomeration of ideas without any satisfying substance. Much of this game feels stilted and unnatural.
Tiling/Mapping is still broken in several spots. Ranging from not being able to pass through something you should be able to, to passing through things you shouldn't be able to. Spacing between where the character can move and where it appears they should be able to move as well.
You can now scan enemies, but now if you use the item on certain enemies it doesn't work. If you use it as the last thing of your turns, it breaks the game.
Some events trigger without telling you who/what/when/where. You can still get the "HELP ME!!" event but no direction as to which way to go to resolve it. The scene were you find Sara, the attacks are going so fast and so much, it's annoying to listen to, but you because you didn't know which direction to run, it may take you a few minutes to finally find and save her. Thankfully she appears indestructible until you go to save her.
While it is nice that there is some kind of "interaction" between the characters when they are just wandering around, it doesn't feel natural or even organic. More of "Oh, you've walked around with me for 300 steps, time to ask me some questions!" The writing needs a lot of work, but also how it's presented stops you and you can't proceed until you make a selection.
Well, at least the awful AI voices got removed.
